For now, forget sensors. Forget timing. There's three things that make an engine run:

  1. Air
  2. Fuel
  3. Spark

So you're definitely not getting one of them. If you weren't getting spark, it wouldn't run at all, not even for a second. But you can verify by pulling each plug one at a time, touching the electrode to a spot on your block, and cranking the key for a second.

If you weren't getting air, it wouldn't start at all, or it would run, but run like a total dog.

If it was a bad sensor, like MAF or O2 or TPS, it would run, but you'd get limp-home mode and a bunch of trouble codes. If you had a bad gasket and were sucking air from somewhere you shouldn't be as someone else suggested, again, it would run, but it would run like shit, and you'd be getting trouble codes from both your MAF and O2 sensors.

That leaves fuel, and you are getting it, but only for a short time.

The longer the car sits, the longer it will run before stalling.

You got shit in your fuel lines. Probably rust from the tank. (Not out of the question on a 20+yr old vehicle.) Even if it's a plastic tank, there's still metal fittings, the sending unit and pickup tubes are metal, the pump internals are metal... I'm not sure how long they kept this theory, but Ford, for a long time, used two fuel pumps - a low pressure/high volume pump inside the tank which then fed a high pressure pump mounted somewhere inline but out on the frame, right behind your fuel filter.

If it sits, the system slowly depressurizes, gravity does its thing, and the shit settles to the bottoms of the lines/rails. Start it back up, the system re-pressurizes, fuel flows momentarily, stirring everything back up, and eventually clogging your injectors again. It would also explain why it stalls if you try to give it gas - everything gets pushed to the injectors where they end up getting clogged.

This is going to be a lot of work, but it sounds like you're no stranger to it:

  • Take the rails and injectors off the engine. Soak it all in kerosene (or even clean gas) overnight.
  • Take the plastic tips off the injectors (assuming it has them) and gently scrub the nozzle with a small wire brush (brass, preferably, but steel if it's all you have). Also clean the end where they connect to the rail. Notice there's a little screen inside that should catch any particulate that makes it past your filters. Again, and I can't stress this enough - be gentle!
  • While you have everything taken apart, put a receptacle of some kind under the fuel line and pulse your key a couple times to cycle the pump. Get that shit out of the lines.
  • Change your in-line fuel filter. Most estimates say 20K to 40K miles. (20K is about what I put on a car in a year, so I just do it every Spring.)
  • Keep in mind that there's also a filter in the fuel tank at the end of the pick up. That one could be compromised, too, and it sounds like it may be. You might want to consider dropping your tank and getting it cleaned, or at least flushing it out.
  • Replace all the o-rings on your injectors, and make sure not to skimp out on them - there's regular o-rings at the hardware store that are pennies apiece, and then there's ones rated for use with gasoline that cost you a couple bucks a pop. Truthfully, you should replace them every single time you pop the injectors out of the intake or rails.

If you don't want to do all that, at the very least, pop your injectors out of the intake and off the rails, set the rails into a receptacle, and run your pump for at least 5 or 10 seconds, then put it all back together. I'd take the opportunity to change those o-rings while you have it apart.
